claim: 4EHP is a key component of the mammalian miRNA-Induced Silencing Complex (miRISC), which mediates gene silencing.
source: We recently discovered that the cap-binding protein 4EHP is a key component of the mammalian miRNA-Induced Silencing Complex (miRISC), which mediates gene silencing.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work (Chapat et al., 2017) and is presented as an established finding.

claim: Dusp6 mRNA, which encodes an ERK1/2 phosphatase, is translationally repressed by 4EHP and miR-145.
source: We show that the Dusp6 mRNA, which encodes an ERK1/2 phosphatase, is translationally repressed by 4EHP and a specific miRNA, miR-145.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript including ribosome profiling, polysome profiling, and luciferase reporter assays.

claim: Translational repression of Dusp6 by 4EHP and miR-145 promotes ERK1/2 phosphorylation.
source: This promotes ERK1/2 phosphorylation, resulting in augmented cell growth and reduced apoptosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data showing ERK1/2 phosphorylation levels in WT vs 4EHP-KO cells.

claim: Translational repression of Dusp6 by 4EHP and miR-145 results in augmented cell growth.
source: This promotes ERK1/2 phosphorylation, resulting in augmented cell growth and reduced apoptosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell proliferation assays showing differences between WT and 4EHP-KO cells.

claim: Translational repression of Dusp6 by 4EHP and miR-145 results in reduced apoptosis.
source: This promotes ERK1/2 phosphorylation, resulting in augmented cell growth and reduced apoptosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS analysis showing sub-G1 populations in 4EHP-depleted cells.

claim: eIF4F is a three-subunit complex composed of eIF4E, eIF4G, and eIF4A.
source: eIF4F is a three-subunit complex composed of eIF4E, the m7GpppN (cap)-interacting factor; eIF4G, a scaffolding protein, and eIF4A, a DEAD-box RNA helicase (Sonenberg and Hinnebusch, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature (Sonenberg and Hinnebusch, 2009).

claim: 4EHP shares 28% sequence identity with eIF4E.
source: 4EHP shares 28% sequence identity with eIF4E (Rom et al., 1998)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rom et al., 1998.

claim: 4EHP is 5–10 times less abundant than eIF4E in most cell types.
source: 4EHP shares 28% sequence identity with eIF4E (Rom et al., 1998) and is ubiquitously expressed, although it is 5–10 times less abundant than eIF4E in most cell types (Joshi et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Joshi et al., 2004.

claim: 4EHP binds the cap with 30- to 100-fold weaker affinity than eIF4E.
source: 4EHP binds the cap with 30- to 100-fold weaker affinity than eIF4E, but its affinity is increased by interactions with other proteins such as 4E-T or post-translational modification (Chapat et al., 2017; Okumura et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chapat et al., 2017 and Okumura et al., 2007.

claim: 4EHP is involved in translational repression directed by miRNAs.
source: 4EHP is involved in translational repression directed by miRNAs (Chapat et al., 2017; Chen and Gao, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chapat et al., 2017 and Chen and Gao, 2017.

claim: The miRNA-Induced Silencing Complex (miRISC) recruits the CCR4–NOT complex to effect mRNA translational repression and decay.
source: The miRNA-Induced Silencing Complex (miRISC) recruits the CCR4–NOT complex to effect mRNA translational repression and decay (Jonas and Izaurralde, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jonas and Izaurralde, 2015.

claim: CCR4–NOT recruits DDX6, 4E-T, and 4EHP to suppress cap-dependent mRNA translation.
source: CCR4–NOT in turn recruits DDX6, 4E-T (eIF4E-Transporter; a conserved 4EHP/eIF4E-binding protein) and 4EHP to suppress cap-dependent mRNA translation (Chapat et al., 2017; Jonas and Izaurralde, 2015; Kamenska et al., 2014; Kamenska et al., 2016; Ozgur et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Chapat et al., 2017; Jonas and Izaurralde, 2015; Kamenska et al., 2014; Kamenska et al., 2016; Ozgur et al., 2015).

claim: DUSP6 is a highly specific phosphatase for ERK1/2.
source: Dual Specificity Phosphatase 6 (DUSP6), also called MAP Kinase Phosphatase-3 (MKP-3), is a highly specific phosphatase for ERK1/2 (Caunt and Keyse, 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Caunt and Keyse, 2013.

claim: DUSP6 is a key player in ERK signaling regulatory feedback loops.
source: Dual Specificity Phosphatase 6 (DUSP6), also called MAP Kinase Phosphatase-3 (MKP-3), is a highly specific phosphatase for ERK1/2 (Caunt and Keyse, 2013) and a key player in ERK signaling regulatory feedback loops (Camps et al., 1998; Eblaghie et al., 2003; Kolch, 2005; Mendoza et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Camps et al., 1998; Eblaghie et al., 2003; Kolch, 2005; Mendoza et al., 2011.

claim: Dusp6-/- mice exhibit increased ERK1/2 phosphorylation at Thr202/Tyr204 residues.
source: Dusp6-/- mice exhibit increased ERK1/2 phosphorylation at Thr202/Tyr204 residues (Li et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Li et al., 2007.

claim: Translation was up-regulated for 117 mRNAs in 4EHP-KO in comparison to WT cells.
source: Translation was up-regulated for 117 mRNAs (hereafter referred to as upregulated mRNAs) in 4EHP-KO in comparison to WT cells, while translation was down-regulated for 167 mRNAs (Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by ribosome profiling data analyzed with the Babel tool, as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Translation was down-regulated for 167 mRNAs in 4EHP-KO in comparison to WT cells.
source: Translation was up-regulated for 117 mRNAs (hereafter referred to as upregulated mRNAs) in 4EHP-KO in comparison to WT cells, while translation was down-regulated for 167 mRNAs (Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by ribosome profiling data analyzed with the Babel tool, as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: mRNAs with longer 3´ UTR are more likely to be translationally repressed by 4EHP.
source: This indicates that mRNAs with longer 3´ UTR are more likely to be translationally repressed by 4EHP.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing correlation between 3' UTR length and translational upregulation in 4EHP-KO cells (Figure 1B).

claim: A significant positive correlation was observed between the length of the 3′ UTR and increased translation of the upregulated mRNAs in the 4EHP-KO cells.
source: A significant positive correlation was observed between the length of the 3′ UTR and increased translation of the upregulated mRNAs in the 4EHP-KO cells (average of 2838.6, 2325.2, and 2016 nt for the up-regulated, unchanged and down-regulated mRNAs, respectively; p-value<2.2e-16; Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of 3' UTR lengths with p-value<2.2e-16, as shown in Figure 1B.

claim: mRNAs which exhibit increased translation in 4EHP-KO cells contained significantly more predicted miRNA-binding sites.
source: mRNAs which exhibit increased translation in 4EHP-KO cells, contained significantly more predicted miRNA-binding sites (642.8, 518.4, and 442.6 for the up-regulated, unchanged and down-regulated mRNAs, respectively; p-values: 0.0004, Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis of miRNA-binding sites with p-value of 0.0004, as shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Slc35e1 and Klhl21 mRNAs were significantly enriched in eIF4E IP in 4EHP-KO cells in comparison with WT.
source: Slc35e1 and Klhl21 but not Tmed7 mRNAs were significantly enriched in eIF4E IP in 4EHP-KO cells in comparison with WT (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA immunoprecipitation (RIP) data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: 4EHP blocks the physical association of its target mRNAs with eIF4E.
source: These data show increased binding of eIF4E to the up-regulated mRNAs in 4EHP-KO cells, and indicate that 4EHP blocks the physical association of its target mRNAs with eIF4E.
evidence: This claim is inferred from RIP data showing increased eIF4E binding to target mRNAs in 4EHP-KO cells.

claim: 4EHP-KO MEFs grew significantly slower than their WT counterparts under standard cell culture conditions.
source: However, at variance with these findings, we found that 4EHP-KO MEFs grew significantly slower than their WT counterparts (48 ± 3% less on day 6; p=0.002) under standard cell culture conditions (5% CO2 and 20% O2) (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure Supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell proliferation assay data shown in Figure 2A with p=0.002.

claim: The slow proliferation of 4EHP-KO cell populations is likely due to a decrease of the percentage of cells in S phase.
source: Cell cycle analysis by FACS showed that the slow proliferation of 4EHP-KO cell populations is likely due to a decrease of the percentage of cells in S phase (30.3% and 21.4% for WT and KO cells, respectively; p=0.003), concomitant with an increase in the G0/G1 phase, compared with WT cells (50.2% and 57.7% for WT and KO cells, respectively; p=0.004, Figure 2—figure Supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure Supplement 1C with p=0.003.

claim: Depletion of 4EHP by shRNAs caused a dramatic reduction in proliferation of U251 human glioblastoma cell lines.
source: Consistently, depletion of 4EHP by shRNAs caused a dramatic reduction in proliferation of U251 (<90% at day 4; Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure Supplement 1D), and U-87 human glioblastoma cell lines (Figure 2—figure Supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell proliferation assay data shown in Figure 2B and supplementary figures.

claim: Depletion of 4EHP in U251 cells increased the fraction of cells in sub-G1, which is associated with apoptosis.
source: Notably, FACS analysis showed that unlike in MEFs, depletion of 4EHP in U251 cells increased the fraction of cells in sub-G1, which is associated with apoptosis (shCTR: 0.9%, sh4EHP#1: 15.5%, and sh4EHP#2: 11.4; Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure Supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 4EHP depletion in U251 cells induced the accumulation of cleaved-PARP, a marker of apoptosis.
source: Accordingly, 4EHP depletion in U251 cells also induced the accumulation of cleaved-PARP (C-PARP), a marker of apoptosis (Figure 2—figure Supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure Supplement 1D.

claim: ERK1/2 phosphorylation was more than 80% reduced in 4EHP-KO MEFs in comparison with WT.
source: While RPS6 phosphorylation remained unchanged, ERK1/2 phosphorylation (Thr202/Tyr204; pERK) was more than 80% reduced in 4EHP-KO MEFs in comparison with WT (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Phosphorylation of MEK remained unchanged in 4EHP-depleted cells.
source: However, phosphorylation of MEK, the immediate upstream kinase of ERK1/2, remained unchanged in 4EHP-depleted cells (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure Supplement 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure Supplement 1H.

claim: The Dusp6 mRNA was shifted towards heavier fractions in the 4EHP-KO cells, demonstrating augmented initiation.
source: While the distribution of the Gapdh mRNA along the sucrose gradient was similar in 4EHP-KO and WT cells, the Dusp6 mRNA was shifted towards heavier fractions in the 4EHP-KO cells (Figure 2E), demonstrating augmented initiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by polysome profiling data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: DUSP6 protein amount was markedly increased in 4EHP-KO MEF as compared to WT.
source: Consistent with greater translation efficiency, DUSP6 protein amount was markedly increased in 4EHP-KO MEF as compared to WT (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Up-regulation of DUSP6 protein level was observed in U251 cells upon 4EHP knockdown in comparison with shCTR-treated cells.
source: Up-regulation of DUSP6 protein level was also observed in U251 cells upon 4EHP knockdown in comparison with shCTR-treated cells (Figure 2—figure Supplement 1K).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure Supplement 1K.

claim: Expression of DUSP7 was not affected by 4EHP depletion.
source: In contrast, expression of DUSP7, another member of the DUSP phosphatase family, was not affected by 4EHP depletion (Figure 2—figure Supplement 1L), attesting to the specificity of 4EHP loss for mRNA translation.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure Supplement 1L.

claim: 4EHP depletion did not affect the abundance of Dusp6 mRNA.
source: 4EHP depletion did not affect the abundance (Figure 2—figure Supplement 1M) or stability of Dusp6 mRNA (Figure 2—figure Supplement 1N).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure Supplement 1M.

claim: 4EHP depletion did not affect the stability of Dusp6 mRNA.
source: 4EHP depletion did not affect the abundance (Figure 2—figure Supplement 1M) or stability of Dusp6 mRNA (Figure 2—figure Supplement 1N).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA stability assay data shown in Figure 2—figure Supplement 1N.

claim: Restoring 4EHP expression in 4EHP-KO MEFs significantly reduced DUSP6 protein levels.
source: Importantly, restoring 4EHP expression in 4EHP-KO MEFs significantly reduced DUSP6 protein levels (~3 fold repression; Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: 4EHP controls expression of the ERK1/2 phosphatase DUSP6 at the level of mRNA translation initiation.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that 4EHP controls expression of the ERK1/2 phosphatase DUSP6 at the level of mRNA translation initiation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from multiple experimental results including polysome profiling, western blots, and rescue experiments.

claim: An 8-fold enrichment of Dusp6 mRNA was detected in eIF4E IP from 4EHP-KO MEF lysates, as compared to WT.
source: While Dusp6 mRNA levels were not significantly different between the WT and 4EHP-KO cells (Figure 3A; for corresponding WB analysis, see Figure 1—figure Supplement 1D), an 8-fold enrichment of Dusp6 mRNA was detected in eIF4E IP from 4EHP-KO MEF lysates, as compared to WT (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RIP data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Dusp7 mRNA was not enriched in eIF4E IP from 4EHP-KO MEFs lysates.
source: As control, Dusp7 mRNA was not enriched in eIF4E IP from 4EHP-KO MEFs lysates.
evidence: This claim is supported by RIP data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The 3´ UTR of Dusp6 mRNA caused a 3-fold repression in comparison with the backbone reporter alone in siCTR-transfected cells.
source: In the siCTR-transfected cells, the 3´ UTR of Dusp6 mRNA caused a 3-fold repression in comparison with the backbone reporter alone (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Knockdown of 4EHP, CNOT1, and 4E-T significantly de-repressed the psiCHECK-Dusp6-3´ UTR reporter.
source: However, knockdown of 4EHP or its partners CNOT1 and 4E-T significantly de-repressed the psiCHECK-Dusp6-3´ UTR reporter (38%, 49%, and 44% respectively as compared to siCTR; Figure 3B), thus supporting the role of CCR4-NOT/4E-T/4EHP pathway in Dusp6 mRNA translational repression.
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Knockdown of CNOT1 and CNOT9 led to an increase of DUSP6 protein amounts in U251 cells.
source: Consistent with the latter results, knockdown of CNOT1 and CNOT9, two critical subunits of the CCR4-NOT complex, also led to an increase of DUSP6 protein amounts in U251 cells (1.4 and 2.2-folds, respectively; Figure 3—figure Supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure Supplement 1A.

claim: A segment of the Dusp6 3' UTR harbouring both miR-145 and miR-181a binding sites exerted the strongest repression on the reporter.
source: A segment harbouring both miR-145 and miR-181a binding sites exerted the strongest repression on the reporter (1.5 fold; p=0001, Figure 3C), which was alleviated upon 4EHP knockdown (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A miR-145 inhibitor increased DUSP6 accumulation to a similar degree as knockdown of 4EHP.
source: While blocking miR-124 and miR-181a did not affect DUSP6 expression, a miR-145 inhibitor increased DUSP6 accumulation to a similar degree as knockdown of 4EHP (Figure 3D), without affecting the stability of the Dusp6 mRNA (Figure 3—figure Supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: miR-145 inhibitor did not affect the stability of the Dusp6 mRNA.
source: While blocking miR-124 and miR-181a did not affect DUSP6 expression, a miR-145 inhibitor increased DUSP6 accumulation to a similar degree as knockdown of 4EHP (Figure 3D), without affecting the stability of the Dusp6 mRNA (Figure 3—figure Supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA stability assay data shown in Figure 3—figure Supplement 1C.

claim: The expression of the reporter containing Dusp6 3´ UTR was significantly de-repressed in the presence of miR-145 inhibitor.
source: Unlike the control reporter, the expression of the reporter containing Dusp6 3´ UTR was significantly de-repressed in the presence of miR-145 inhibitor (1.25 fold repression compared with 2.09 for mock inhibitor; Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Silencing of the Dusp6 3´ UTR reporter was fully reversed in 4EHP-KO HEK293 cells.
source: Consistent with our observation that siRNA depletion of 4EHP in HEK293T cells de-repressed the Dusp6 3´ UTR reporter (Figure 3B), silencing of the same reporter was fully reversed in a 4EHP-KO HEK293 cells (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: No de-repression by the miR-145 inhibitor was observed in 4EHP-KO HEK293 cells.
source: No de-repression by the miR-145 inhibitor was observed in 4EHP-KO HEK293 cells (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: 4EHP is required for miR-145-induced translational silencing of Dusp6 mRNA.
source: This confirms the requirement for 4EHP in miR-145-induced translational silencing of Dusp6 mRNA.
evidence: This claim is inferred from luciferase reporter assay data showing no effect of miR-145 inhibitor in 4EHP-KO cells.

claim: The Dusp6 mRNA translation is controlled by its 3´ UTR through the miRNA/CCR4-NOT/4E-T/4EHP pathway.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that the Dusp6 mRNA translation is controlled by its 3´ UTR through the miRNA/CCR4-NOT/4E-T/4EHP pathway.
evidence: This claim is inferred from multiple experimental results including reporter assays and knockdown experiments.

claim: Treatment of 4EHP-KO cells with BCI increased pERK1/2 to levels comparable with untreated WT cells within 30 min.
source: Treatment of 4EHP-KO cells with BCI increased pERK1/2 to levels comparable with untreated WT cells within 30 min (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot time course data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Reduced ERK1/2 phosphorylation in 4EHP-depleted cells is due to increased DUSP6 activity.
source: These data confirm that reduced ERK1/2 phosphorylation in 4EHP-depleted cells is due to increased DUSP6 activity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from BCI treatment experiments showing rescue of ERK1/2 phosphorylation.

claim: Depletion of DUSP6 in 4EHP-KO cells markedly augmented their proliferation.
source: While DUSP6 knockdown did not have a detectable impact on WT cells proliferation, depletion of DUSP6 in 4EHP-KO cells markedly augmented their proliferation (42% increase for sh4EHP#1 [p=0.007] and 65% increase for sh4EHP#2 [p=0.004] on day 4; Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell proliferation assay data shown in Figure 4B with p-values of 0.007 and 0.004.

claim: The reduced proliferation of 4EHP-KO cells is at least partially due to de-repression of DUSP6.
source: This result demonstrates that the reduced proliferation of 4EHP-KO cells is at least partially due to de-repression of DUSP6.
evidence: This claim is inferred from rescue experiments showing increased proliferation upon DUSP6 knockdown in 4EHP-KO cells.

claim: ERK1/2 phosphorylation remained unchanged in 4EHP-KO MEFs expressing constitutively active KRAS (G12V).
source: While ERK1/2 phosphorylation was increased by forced KRAS activity in WT MEFs, pERK levels remained unchanged in 4EHP-KO MEFs (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: WT MEFs proliferation was slightly increased upon enforced KRAS activity, but remained unaffected in 4EHP-KO MEFs.
source: Consistent with these results, WT MEFs proliferation was slightly increased upon enforced KRAS activity, but remained unaffected in 4EHP-KO MEFs (Figure 4—figure Supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell proliferation assay data shown in Figure 4—figure Supplement 1C.

claim: 4EHP up-regulates ERK1/2 phosphorylation by effecting the miRNA-induced translational repression of Dusp6 mRNA.
source: Taken together, the data demonstrate that 4EHP up-regulates ERK1/2 phosphorylation by effecting the miRNA-induced translational repression of Dusp6 mRNA, and that depletion of 4EHP limits ERK activation by upstream signaling (Figure 4D, model).
evidence: This claim is inferred from multiple experimental results including western blots, reporter assays, and rescue experiments.

claim: Depletion of 4EHP limits ERK activation by upstream signaling.
source: Taken together, the data demonstrate that 4EHP up-regulates ERK1/2 phosphorylation by effecting the miRNA-induced translational repression of Dusp6 mRNA, and that depletion of 4EHP limits ERK activation by upstream signaling (Figure 4D, model).
evidence: This claim is inferred from experiments showing that constitutively active KRAS cannot increase ERK phosphorylation in 4EHP-KO cells.

claim: 4EHP acts as an effector of translational repression instigated by miRNAs.
source: We previously demonstrated that the cap-binding protein 4EHP acts as an effector of translational repression instigated by miRNAs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Translational repression of Dusp6 mRNA by 4EHP and miR-145 occurs in the absence of mRNA decay.
source: Here, we identify Dusp6 mRNA as a functionally critical target of this silencing mechanism, which occurs in the absence of mRNA decay.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA stability assay data showing no change in Dusp6 mRNA stability upon 4EHP depletion.

claim: Translational repression of Dusp6 mRNA by 4EHP and miR-145 down-regulates the MAPK/ERK signaling cascade.
source: Translational repression of Dusp6 mRNA by the combined action of 4EHP and miR-145 down-regulates the MAPK/ERK signaling cascade and its output in cell proliferation and survival.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data showing reduced ERK phosphorylation in 4EHP-KO cells.

claim: The 4EHP/miRNA repression mechanism engenders important biological consequences in homeostasis and disease.
source: The 4EHP/miRNA repression mechanism thus engenders important biological consequences in homeostasis and disease.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed effects on cell proliferation, apoptosis, and ERK signaling.

claim: Several large-scale studies reported that mammalian miRNAs predominantly act by decreasing target mRNA levels.
source: Several large-scale studies reported that mammalian miRNAs predominantly act by decreasing target mRNA levels (Baek et al., 2008; Eichhorn et al., 2014; Guo et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Baek et al., 2008; Eichhorn et al., 2014; Guo et al., 2010.

claim: Some studies showed that miRNAs affect the expression of target genes by translation inhibition.
source: while others showed that miRNAs affect the expression of target genes by translation inhibition (Jin et al., 2017; Selbach et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jin et al., 2017; Selbach et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2009.

claim: Translational repression precedes target mRNA decay.
source: It was convincingly demonstrated in in vitro and in vivo studies that translational repression precedes target mRNA decay (Bazzini et al., 2012; Béthune et al., 2012; Djuranovic et al., 2012; Fabian et al., 2009; Mathonnet et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bazzini et al., 2012; Béthune et al., 2012; Djuranovic et al., 2012; Fabian et al., 2009; Mathonnet et al., 2007.

claim: 4EHP effects miRNA-mediated translational repression of Dusp6 mRNA, but not mRNA stability.
source: Our data demonstrate that 4EHP effects miRNA-mediated translational repression of Dusp6 mRNA, but not mRNA stability.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA stability assay and western blot data.

claim: The relative contribution of translational repression and mRNA degradation to miRNA-mediated silencing may depend on the target mRNAs and on the cellular context.
source: The relative contribution of translational repression and mRNA degradation to miRNA-mediated silencing may thus depend on the target mRNAs and on the cellular context.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Dusp6 shows translational repression without mRNA decay.

claim: The RBPs PUM2 and TTP were implicated in the post-transcriptional repression of Dusp6 mRNA.
source: The RBPs PUM2 and TTP were implicated in the post-transcriptional repression of Dusp6 mRNA, presumably in a CCR4-NOT-dependent mechanism (Bermudez et al., 2011; Galgano et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bermudez et al., 2011 and Galgano et al., 2008.

claim: Indirect up-regulation of ERK1/2 phosphorylation by 4EHP, via repression of Dusp6 translation, explains the diminished cell proliferation in 4EHP-KO MEF cells.
source: Indirect up-regulation of ERK1/2 phosphorylation by 4EHP, via repression of Dusp6 translation, explains the diminished cell proliferation in 4EHP-KO MEF cells and apoptosis observed in 4EHP-depleted U251 and U87 cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from multiple experimental results showing the relationship between 4EHP, DUSP6, ERK phosphorylation, and cell proliferation.

claim: Indirect up-regulation of ERK1/2 phosphorylation by 4EHP, via repression of Dusp6 translation, explains the apoptosis observed in 4EHP-depleted U251 and U87 cells.
source: Indirect up-regulation of ERK1/2 phosphorylation by 4EHP, via repression of Dusp6 translation, explains the diminished cell proliferation in 4EHP-KO MEF cells and apoptosis observed in 4EHP-depleted U251 and U87 cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from FACS data showing increased sub-G1 population and cleaved-PARP in 4EHP-depleted cells.

claim: Constitutively active RAS fails to increase ERK1/2 phosphorylation in 4EHP-KO MEFs.
source: Specifically, constitutively active RAS fails to increase ERK1/2 phosphorylation in 4EHP-KO MEFs.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data showing no increase in pERK upon KRAS G12V expression in 4EHP-KO cells.

claim: Increased DUSP6 expression in 4EHP-KO cells effectively impairs phosphorylation of ERK1/2 downstream of RAS.
source: This can be explained by increased DUSP6 expression in 4EHP-KO cells, which effectively impairs phosphorylation of ERK1/2 downstream of RAS.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that constitutively active RAS cannot increase ERK phosphorylation in 4EHP-KO cells with elevated DUSP6.

claim: Over-expression of constitutively active RAS induces DUSP6 expression constituting a negative feedback loop.
source: Interestingly, over-expression of constitutively active RAS (Park et al., 2014), or BRAF (Agrawal et al., 2014), also induces DUSP6 expression constituting a negative feedback loop.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Park et al., 2014 and Agrawal et al., 2014.

claim: Over-expression of constitutively active BRAF induces DUSP6 expression constituting a negative feedback loop.
source: Interestingly, over-expression of constitutively active RAS (Park et al., 2014), or BRAF (Agrawal et al., 2014), also induces DUSP6 expression constituting a negative feedback loop.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Park et al., 2014 and Agrawal et al., 2014.

claim: The feedback loop restrains the activity of the RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK pathway upon induction by stimuli.
source: The feedback loop restrains the activity of the RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK pathway upon induction by stimuli (e.g. growth factors).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the known function of DUSP6 as an ERK phosphatase and the feedback regulation mechanism.

claim: Increasing DUSP6 expression by inhibiting 4EHP can potentially repress ERK pathway activation.
source: Thus, increasing DUSP6 expression by inhibiting 4EHP can potentially repress ERK pathway activation.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observed relationship between 4EHP, DUSP6, and ERK signaling.

claim: 4EHP contributes to the translational repression activity of a reporter mRNA by let-7 miRNA.
source: We had previously shown that 4EHP contributes to the translational repression activity of a reporter mRNA by let-7 miRNA (Chapat et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chapat et al., 2017.

claim: let-7 miRNA can instigate mRNA deadenylation and decay.
source: but let-7 miRNA can also clearly instigate mRNA deadenylation and decay.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about let-7 miRNA function.

claim: let-7 suppresses tumorigenesis by directly silencing RAS expression.
source: An interesting miRNA to revisit in light of this mechanism is let-7, which suppresses tumorigenesis by directly silencing RAS expression (Johnson et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Johnson et al., 2005.

claim: Binding of the mRNA 5´ cap by 4EHP impairs translation initiation.
source: Binding of the mRNA 5´ cap by the 4E Homologous Protein (4EHP, encoded by Eif4e2), in contrast to eIF4E, impairs translation initiation (Cho et al., 2005; Morita et al., 2012; Rom et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cho et al., 2005; Morita et al., 2012; Rom et al., 1998.

claim: 4EHP is ubiquitously expressed.
source: 4EHP shares 28% sequence identity with eIF4E (Rom et al., 1998) and is ubiquitously expressed
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about 4EHP expression patterns.

claim: 4EHP's affinity for the cap is increased by interactions with other proteins such as 4E-T or post-translational modification.
source: 4EHP binds the cap with 30- to 100-fold weaker affinity than eIF4E, but its affinity is increased by interactions with other proteins such as 4E-T or post-translational modification (Chapat et al., 2017; Okumura et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chapat et al., 2017 and Okumura et al., 2007.

claim: ERK1/2 are important effectors of the highly conserved Mitogen-Activated Protein Kinase (MAPK) signaling pathway.
